title: THE UNTOLD STORY BEHIND JOSHUA MEETING THE COMMANDER OF HEAVEN'S ARMY
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD STORY BEHIND JOSHUA MEETING THE COMMANDER OF HEAVEN'S ARMY
The Night Before Jericho Fell, Joshua Met Someone Who Was Not an Angel.
Across the Jordan stood the city that had haunted Israel for generations.
Its walls towered above the landscape like a declaration of human strength and defiance. Massive. Impenetrable. Ancient.
Tomorrow would begin Israel's first major battle inside the Promised Land.
But that night, Joshua was alone.
Just a leader carrying the weight of an entire nation on his shoulders.
Everything that follows in Joshua 5:13-15 is one of the most mysterious, breathtaking, and often misunderstood encounters in all of Scripture.
Most people know the walls of Jericho fell.
Few know what happened before they fell.
Fewer still understand who Joshua actually met.
And once you see it, you may never read the story the same way again.
The Hebrew text opens with remarkable simplicity:
"Now it came to pass when Joshua was by Jericho..."
Probably doing exactly what every leader does when facing something impossible.
Trying to figure out how to win.
"He lifted up his eyes and looked."
A Man with a sword drawn in His hand.
The Hebrew word for sword is:
A weapon of judgment, warfare, and authority.
This was not a peaceful visitor.
"Are you for us or for our adversaries?" (Joshua 5:13)
It is a question every human heart asks.
Joshua assumes there are only two options.
But the answer shatters the entire framework.
"But I am the Commander of the Army of Yahweh."
The word sar means prince, ruler, captain, commander.
The word tzeva means army, host, heavenly forces.
"I am the Commander of Yahweh's armies."
Notice what He did not say.
"I did not come to take sides.
Joshua's greatest need was not for God to join his mission.
His greatest need was to surrender to God's mission.
That truth still confronts believers today.
"Will you join what God is doing?"
The Commander of Heaven's Army was not there to receive Joshua's strategy.
Joshua was there to receive His.
Many assume this figure was an angel.
The text refuses to let us stop there.
The moment Joshua hears who He is, he falls face down and worships.
"Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped."
means bowing in worship, reverence, and submission.
Throughout Scripture faithful angels reject worship.
When the Apostle John fell before an angel, the angel immediately replied:
"Do not do that! I am a fellow servant."
Yet here there is no correction.
"Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy."
Because those are almost the exact words spoken to Moses at the burning bush.
Holy ground only exists because God's presence is there.
Angels do not make ground holy.
Many biblical scholars throughout church history have identified this figure as what theologians call a Christophany.
A pre-incarnate appearance of Jesus Christ before Bethlehem.
Not Jesus in His earthly body.
But the eternal Son revealing Himself before the incarnation.
Several clues point in this direction.
He appears as God yet is distinct from the Father.
This pattern appears elsewhere in the Old Testament through the mysterious figure known as:
But the Messenger who speaks as God, receives worship, and reveals God.
Many theologians believe Joshua was standing face-to-face with the same eternal Christ who later would walk the roads of Galilee.
The same Jesus who would calm storms.
And ultimately go to the cross.
Before Joshua ever entered battle, he encountered the true King.
The Commander arrives before Jericho falls.
God could have appeared after the victory.
Instead He appears before any success happens.
Because Joshua needed something greater than victory.
The greatest gift was never the falling walls.
The greatest gift was the One standing in front of him.
Many believers spend their lives chasing God's intervention.
The miracle was not the walls falling.
The miracle was the Commander appearing.
THE NIGHT JOSHUA STOPPED BEING THE HERO
But in this moment Scripture quietly removes him from center stage.
Joshua enters the scene as commander of Israel's army.
He leaves the scene as a servant receiving orders.
The story is not about Joshua's greatness.
The Bible was never primarily about great men doing great things.
It is about a great God accomplishing His purposes through surrendered people.
Joshua's success began the moment he realized he was not the highest-ranking authority on the battlefield.
Many people today are standing outside their own Jericho.
And like Joshua, they are staring at walls that seem impossible.
But perhaps the better question is:
The Commander of Heaven's Army still confronts human pride.
Still reminds us that battles are won not by human strength but by divine authority.
Before Jericho fell outwardly, Joshua bowed inwardly.
That is where every genuine victory begins.
The older you get, the more you realize that some walls are not defeated by strength.
They fall when you finally kneel.
Maybe that's why this story survives generation after generation.
Because every believer eventually discovers that the greatest breakthrough comes after surrender, not before it.
One night before the walls fell, Joshua discovered the battle was never his to carry.
And maybe the wall in front of you is waiting for the same realization.
